extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners, and USPTO examiners (AI/ET stakeholders)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining inventorship and related patent-practice requirements when AI systems assist in creating inventions, focusing on when natural persons qualify as inventors and how to handle filings and prosecution. Applies to utility, plant, and design patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted inventions not categorically unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: AI assisted inventions are not categorically unpatentable for improper inventorship; use of an AI system (or other advanced tools) by a natural person(s) does not preclude that natural person(s) from qualifying as the inventor (or joint inventors) if the natural person(s) significantly contributed to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus of inventorship analysis is on the human contributions, specifically whether they meet the Pannu factors. Applications and patents must not list any entity that is not a natural person as the inventor or joint inventor, even if an AI system may have been instrumental in the creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only natural persons may be named as inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications and patents must name the natural person(s) who significantly contributed to the invention as the inventor or joint inventors; cannot list entities or AI systems as inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 115 requires the patent application to name the inventor(s). Inventors named on the application data sheet (ADS) or oath/declaration are presumed to be the actual inventors. No oath, declaration, or substitute statement should be filed on behalf of an AI system. Assignments from AI systems should not be recorded with the USPTO because an AI system cannot be a named inventor and has no rights to assign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pannu factor 1 — significant contribution to conception (or reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each named inventor must contribute in some significant manner to the conception or reduction to practice of the invention — i.e., significantly contribute to the 'definite and permanent idea of the complete and operative invention as it is thereafter applied in practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception analysis focuses on natural person(s) contributions. Reduction to practice of an invention conceived by another is not enough to constitute inventorship. Reference to reduction to practice acknowledges simultaneous conception/reduction-to-practice doctrine in unpredictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pannu factor 2 — contribution quality not insignificant
rubrics_metrics.description: Each named inventor must make a contribution to the claimed invention that is not insignificant in quality, when that contribution is measured against the dimension of the full invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing routine or expected inputs to an AI system could be an exercise of normal skill and be considered insignificant in quality. Selection of well-known materials or routine choices are examples of contributions likely insignificant when measured against the full invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pannu factor 3 — more than merely explaining state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor must do more than merely explain to the real inventors well-known concepts and/or the current state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experts consulted only to discuss current state of the art, who were not involved in the invention creation process, would likely not satisfy this factor. Mere explanation or teaching of known concepts is insufficient (see Fina Oil & Chemical Co. v. Ewen and Hess v. Advanced Cardiovascular Sys.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to meet any Pannu factor precludes inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet any one of the three Pannu factors precludes that person from being named the inventor or joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis is claim-by-claim and case-by-case. Joint inventors may apply even though each did not make the same type or amount of contribution or did not contribute to every claim; however, each claim must have at least one natural person inventor. When a single person uses an AI system to create an invention, that person must make a significant contribution to every claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim and case-by-case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the Pannu factors to determine whether a natural person significantly contributed to an AI-assisted invention is made on a claim-by-claim and case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No requirement that each named joint inventor contribute to every claim — a contribution to a single claim is sufficient — but each claim must have at least one natural person inventor. Each inventor must make a significant contribution to conception, and at least one inventor must have recognition and appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp1 — use of AI does not negate human contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural person’s use of an AI system in creating an AI-assisted invention does not negate the person’s contributions as an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when AI played an instrumental role, a human who made a qualifying contribution remains eligible to be named as inventor if Pannu factors are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp2 — recognizing problem vs. conception; prompt construction may matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely recognizing a problem or having a general goal or research plan to pursue does not rise to the level of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A natural person who only presents a problem to an AI system may not be a proper inventor of an invention identified from the AI output. However, a significant contribution could be shown in how the person constructs the prompt in view of a specific problem to elicit a particular solution from the AI system — prompt construction tailored to elicit a specific inventive solution can be significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp3 — reduction to practice alone is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to practice alone is not a significant contribution that rises to the level of inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who merely recognizes and appreciates the output of an AI system as an invention, particularly when the properties and utility are apparent to those of ordinary skill, is not necessarily an inventor. However, a person who takes the output and makes a significant contribution to the output to create an invention may be a proper inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp4 — essential building block developers may be inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural person who develops an essential building block from which the claimed invention is derived may be considered to have provided a significant contribution to the conception of the claimed invention even though not present for each activity that led to conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some situations, the person who designs, builds, or trains an AI system in view of a specific problem to elicit a particular solution could be an inventor, where that designing/building/training is a significant contribution to the invention created with the AI system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp5 — intellectual domination alone does not confer inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining 'intellectual domination' over an AI system does not, on its own, make a person an inventor of any inventions created through the use of the AI system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply owning or overseeing an AI system used in creation, without providing a significant contribution to conception, does not make that person an inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor’s oath/declaration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Named inventors must execute an oath or declaration unless a substitute statement is submitted on their behalf; only natural persons may execute such statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not file an oath, declaration, or substitute statement on behalf of an AI system. Inventors named on the ADS or oath/declaration are presumed to be the actual inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of disclosure and duty of reasonable inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants and parties have a duty of disclosure (information material to patentability) and a duty of reasonable inquiry when presenting papers to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties apply to parties identified in 37 CFR §§ 1.56(c), 1.555(a), and 42.11(a). Reasonable inquiry certification (37 CFR 11.18(b)) could include questions about whether and how AI is being used in the invention creation process. See MPEP 2004 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner requests under 37 CFR § 1.105 and possible rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may request information under 37 CFR § 1.105 (MPEP § 704.10); information need not be material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may request information when there is a reasonable basis to conclude a party has information reasonably necessary to examination. Examples include when inventorship is unclear because evidence suggests a human did not significantly contribute while natural persons are named, contradictory statements by applicant, or when facts support a prima facie case that named inventor(s) did not contribute significantly. When such a prima facie case exists, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of inventorship procedures and remedy when no natural inventor exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When contributions by a named inventor do not rise to the level of inventorship, inventorship must be corrected by proper regulatory mechanisms; when no natural person significantly contributed, claims must be canceled or amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventorship error in patent applications: 37 CFR § 1.48(a) or by filing a continuing application under 37 CFR § 1.53 and abandoning the parent. Inventorship error in issued patents: 37 CFR § 1.324 or reissue. Applicants have a continued duty to ensure proper listing of inventorship during prosecution due to claim amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit/priority claims when foreign application names non-natural persons
rubrics_metrics.description: For a U.S. application claiming priority to a foreign application that names both a natural person(s) and a non-natural person as a joint inventor, the U.S. ADS must list only the natural person(s) who significantly contributed to the invention and one of those natural persons must be in common with the foreign application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents importing a non-natural inventor into the U.S. application; ensure the priority chain includes a common natural person inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments from AI systems should not be recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments from AI systems should not be recorded with the USPTO because an AI system cannot be a named inventor and has no rights to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records of assignment must reflect only assignable interests held by natural persons or legal entities that derive rights via proper inventorship/assignment pathways; AI systems have neither inventorship nor assignable rights.
